challenges.name: enrollment-rules-quiz
challenges.title: Where do the enrollment rules hold?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the duplicate-enrollment incident: two requests that both passed the service's duplicate check, and a reactivation that skipped the entitlement check.

questions.explanation: True. The two requests started 3 ms apart and each took over 30 ms, so both ran findByUserAndCourse before either inserted: both saw no row, both passed the check and both called create. A check-then-insert in application code is a race whenever two requests overlap, and only the database can make the second insert fail, with UNIQUE (user_id, course_id) (the race and the constraint are covered in "Stop duplicate enrollment: races & unique constraints" in SQL & Data Modeling). The service rule is still worth having: it answers the common sequential retry with a clean "existing" result and a good error message, and the repository turns the rare unique violation (SQLSTATE 23505) into the same answer. The misconception is that a rule in the service is enough on its own because each request is handled correctly in isolation.

False. The rules describe the state at the time of the request, not at the time of the first enrollment. Since then u_5002 was refunded and lost the entitlement, so this path gives the premium course back for free. The same applies to a course that was unpublished, or that gained a prerequisite, after the learner cancelled. A reactivation is a new decision: run the published, prerequisite and entitlement checks first, then flip the status of the existing row, which keeps one row per learner and course. The only request that may skip the rules is a repeat of one that already succeeded, which is what returning an active enrollment does. The misconception is treating "was allowed once" as "is allowed now".

challenges.name: enrollment-service-rules
challenges.title: EnrollmentService: no duplicates, prerequisites first
challenges.description:
POST /enrollments on the CodeDev API calls EnrollmentService.enroll(userId, courseId). The shipped version inserted a row for every request, so a double tap and a mobile retry left learners enrolled twice, and the prerequisite check only existed in the web client. Write enroll so the rules live in the service. The repositories are injected through the constructor (in production they are backed by PostgreSQL; here they are in-memory fakes) and, like rows read from a database, every object they return is a copy: a change is stored only when you pass the object to enrollments.save().

Check the rules in this order. 1) courses.findById(courseId) returns undefined: throw new CourseNotFoundError(courseId). 2) The learner has an enrollment in this course with status "active": return { outcome: "existing", enrollment } with that enrollment and check nothing else (a repeated request gets the same answer even if the course was unpublished or its rules changed since). 3) course.published is false: throw new CourseNotPublishedError(courseId). 4) Some courses in course.prerequisites are not completed by the learner (completions.hasCompleted): throw new PrerequisitesMissingError(courseId, missing) with all of them, in the order of course.prerequisites. 5) course.premium is true and entitlements.hasEntitlement(userId, courseId) is false: throw new EntitlementRequiredError(courseId). 6) The learner has a "cancelled" enrollment in this course: set its status to "active", save it and return { outcome: "reactivated", enrollment } (same id, never a second row). 7) Otherwise return { outcome: "created", enrollment: enrollments.create(userId, courseId) }.

Input (stdin): { "courses": [{ id, published, premium, prerequisites }], "completions": [[userId, courseId]], "entitlements": [[userId, courseId]], "enrollments": [{ id, userId, courseId, status }], "operations": [{ "op": "enroll" | "cancel", userId, courseId }], "summary"?: true }. Ids are compared exactly (no trimming, case-sensitive). "cancel" is done by the test runner on the repository. Output: one line per operation (the outcome with the enrollment id and status, or "error <code>" with the missing prerequisites in brackets), then every enrollment row ordered by id; with summary, only the count per outcome or error code and the number of active and cancelled rows. Do not change the types, error classes, repositories or test runner.
hints: For each request, ask two questions in this order: has this exact request already succeeded before (then the answer must not change), and if not, would the rules let this learner in right now?

Look at what findByUserAndCourse returns - undefined, an active enrollment or a cancelled one - and at where each of the three cases has to leave the function relative to the published, prerequisite and entitlement checks. For the prerequisites, collect every course that fails instead of stopping at the first. An object from the repository is a copy until it goes through save().

A similar service for workshop seats: register(userId, workshopId) returns the existing seat for a confirmed registration without checking anything else; a learner missing two of the three required badges [git, sql, docker] gets an error listing [git, docker], not only [git]; a withdrawn registration has its capacity and badges checked again, and only then is { ...registration, status: "confirmed" } saved under the same id.
